title: Pigeonhole Principle
quickIdea: A guarantee, not a probability: to force r objects into some one box out of k, you need k(r-1)+1 objects.
remember: Simple form: n+1 objects in n boxes puts two in one box.
Generalised: N objects in k boxes puts at least ceil(N/k) in some box.
Guarantee form: to force r in some box you need k(r-1)+1 objects.
Method: negate the claim; if the negation is realisable the claim fails.
Negation rules: not(x >= n) is x <= n-1; not(x <= n) is x >= n+1.

example.prompt: Cards from a 52-card deck to guarantee 3 of one suit.
example.work: Worst case 2 per suit = 8 cards with no suit at 3, so the next card forces it.

gateAngle: GATE CS 2000 asks exactly this (answer 9). 'Minimum number to guarantee' is always worst case plus one, never an average.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many integers must you pick from {1,...,20} to guarantee two that sum to 21?
variations.why: The pairs are {1,20}, {2,19}, ..., {10,11} - 10 boxes. Picking 10 could take one from each pair, so 11 forces a complete pair.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: 13 people are in a room. Must two share a birth month?
variations.why: 12 months are the boxes and 13 people are the pigeons, so some month holds at least ceil(13/12) = 2 people. No probability is involved.

trap.what: Treating a high probability as a guarantee, or reading 'exactly k' as 'at least k'.
trap.why: The pigeonhole principle gives certainty from counting alone, and it only pins a lower bound. 'Some box has exactly k' can be false while 'some box has at least k' is guaranteed.
trap.counterexample: With 9 cards you are guaranteed 3 of one suit, but you are not guaranteed a suit with exactly 3 - the split could be 3,2,2,2 or even 4,2,2,1.

check.question: How many people guarantee that two share a birth month?
check.explanation: 12 months, so 12 people could all differ; the 13th must repeat a month.
